title: Liberalism and Its Communitarian Critics
subtitle: Are we choosers standing apart from our ends, or selves made by our communities?
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain what liberal neutrality and the priority of the right over the good mean
By the end you will be able to reconstruct Sandel's critique of the 'unencumbered self' and Taylor's case against atomism
By the end you will be able to describe Walzer's spheres of justice and MacIntyre's critique of modern moral culture
By the end you will be able to assess Rawls's political liberalism as a reply, and the liberal counter-arguments
hook:
Imagine filling in a form that asks: *Who are you?* You might write your name and job. But think harder. You are someone's daughter or son. You speak a language you did not choose, which shapes the very thoughts you think. You may belong to a faith, a town, a nation with a long memory. Could you strip all of that away and still have a self left over to do the choosing?

On Day 82 you met John Rawls's veil of ignorance, behind which we choose principles of justice without knowing our sex, class, religion or idea of the good life. It is one of the most influential thought experiments of the twentieth century. Within a decade, a group of philosophers answered that the person behind the veil is a fiction, and a dangerous one. They became known, somewhat against their will, as the **communitarians**. Their quarrel with liberalism is still being fought, now in elections rather than journals.

sections.heading: What Liberals Claim
sections.body:
**Liberalism** in political philosophy does not mean 'left-wing' as in American usage. It names a broad tradition, from Locke and Kant through Mill to Rawls, built around individual freedom, equal rights and limited government. Two ideas are central to the version the communitarians attacked.

The first is the **priority of the right over the good**. 'The good' means a conception of what makes life worthwhile: a religious path, a life of art, family, adventure. 'The right' means principles of justice: fair terms on which people with different conceptions of the good can live together. For Rawls, justice comes first. Your pursuit of the good must operate within the limits justice sets, and justice must not be designed to favour any one vision of the good life.

The second is **state neutrality**. The government should not promote one way of life as better than others. It protects your freedom to pursue whatever good you choose, so long as you respect others' equal freedom. A liberal state does not tell you whether to pray, how to marry or what to value; it guarantees a fair framework within which you decide.

Behind both ideas lies a picture of the person. Rawls wrote in *A Theory of Justice* (1971) that the self is prior to the ends which are affirmed by it. In other words, *you* are distinct from your goals. You can step back, examine any commitment, and revise it. That capacity to choose and revise your ends is what liberalism protects above all.

sections.heading: Sandel: The Unencumbered Self
sections.body:
In *Liberalism and the Limits of Justice* (1982), the Harvard philosopher **Michael Sandel** argued that this picture of the person cannot be true of us, and that liberalism depends on it.

Sandel called Rawls's chooser the **unencumbered self**: a self defined prior to and independent of any attachments, which then picks its ends as a shopper picks goods. Against this he set the **encumbered** or **situated self**, partly constituted by its attachments. Some of our ends are not things we *have* but part of what we *are*. Sandel called these **constitutive attachments**. A person who loses her faith, or her sense of belonging to a family or nation, does not simply change preferences; in an important sense she becomes a different person.

Why does this matter politically? Sandel offered two arguments.

First, the unencumbered self cannot explain obligations we did not choose. Many people feel duties of loyalty and solidarity, to family, community or country, that do not come from any contract. On the liberal picture these seem irrational. Sandel thinks they are some of our deepest moral experiences.

Second, Rawls's difference principle (the rule that inequalities are permitted only if they benefit the worst off) treats people's talents as a **common asset** whose fruits may be shared. But why should *I* share my talents with *you* unless we already form a community bound together in some thick sense? Sandel argued that Rawls's own conclusions quietly presuppose the kind of community his theory of the self denies.

The liberal reply, pressed by Will Kymlicka, is that Sandel confuses two claims. Liberals need not say we can stand outside *all* our ends at once, only that we can question *any particular* end. A Catholic can come to doubt her faith; a nationalist can come to see his nation's crimes. Our ability to revise even deep commitments is real and precious, and that is what liberalism protects.

sections.heading: Taylor: Against Atomism, For Recognition
sections.body:
The Canadian philosopher **Charles Taylor**, from Montreal, has spent his career between English and French Canada, a background that shows in his interest in language and identity. In an essay called *Atomism* (1979), he attacked a strand of liberal thought that treats individuals as self-sufficient units who form society only for convenience, as in Hobbes's state of nature (Day 42).

Taylor's point is that the very capacities liberals prize, choosing freely, reflecting critically, forming a life plan, are not given by nature. They are developed only within a certain kind of society: one with languages rich enough for reflection, cultures that offer meaningful options, institutions like schools and free presses. If you value autonomy, you must also value, and help sustain, the society that makes autonomy possible. Rights cannot have absolute priority over obligations to belong.

In *Sources of the Self* (1989) Taylor added that identity is **dialogical**: we discover who we are through conversation with others, using languages of value we inherit. No one can define themselves from scratch.

This led to his influential essay *The Politics of Recognition* (1992). If identity is formed in dialogue, then being misrecognised, seen through a demeaning picture by others, can be a real harm. Taylor asked whether a liberal state could legitimately act to preserve a culture, for instance Quebec's laws promoting the French language. Strict neutrality would forbid this. Taylor argued for a more hospitable liberalism that protects fundamental rights for all while allowing a society to pursue collective goals, like cultural survival, so long as it respects those who do not share them.

sections.heading: Walzer: Spheres of Justice
sections.body:
**Michael Walzer** of Princeton took a different route in *Spheres of Justice* (1983). His target was the method of theories like Rawls's: finding universal principles by abstract reasoning from a standpoint outside any society. Walzer proposed instead that justice is a matter of interpreting the **shared meanings** that goods have within a particular community.

Consider different goods: medical care, political office, money, love, honours, education. Walzer argued that each has its own social meaning, and so its own proper principle of distribution. Medical care, in modern societies, is understood as something owed to the sick according to need. Prizes are given for merit. Commodities are traded on markets. Political power is distributed by persuasion and votes.

Injustice, for Walzer, occurs when one good *dominates* others, when success in one sphere buys success in another where it does not belong. Money buying votes, political connections buying university places, wealth buying better justice in the courts: these are violations of the boundaries between spheres. His ideal is **complex equality**: not that everyone has the same amount of everything, but that no single good converts into all the others.

Walzer listed **blocked exchanges**, things that money may not buy in a just society: votes, exemption from military service, court verdicts, public office, basic freedoms, friendship and love.

This is powerful, but it raises a worry. If justice is relative to a society's shared meanings, can we criticise a caste society whose members share the understanding that caste determines worth? Walzer answered that social meanings are rarely as unified as they look, and that internal critics can always appeal to a society's own deepest ideals against its practices. Critics doubt this is enough.

sections.heading: MacIntyre: Traditions, Practices and Narrative
sections.body:
The most radical of the group is **Alasdair MacIntyre**, born in Scotland in 1929, who passed through Marxism before arriving at Aristotle and Thomas Aquinas. You met his *After Virtue* (1981) on Day 85 as part of the revival of virtue ethics. Its politics are just as important.

MacIntyre opens with an unsettling parable: imagine a future in which natural science has been destroyed and later reconstructed from fragments, with people using words like 'neutrino' without understanding the theories that gave them meaning. Our moral language, he suggests, is in that state. We use words like 'rights', 'duty' and 'virtue' as fragments of older traditions, especially Aristotle's, without the framework that made them intelligible. That is why modern moral debates about war, abortion or inequality are interminable: rival sides start from incommensurable premises and have no shared way of settling them.

Against the liberal self, MacIntyre offers a **narrative** conception: a human life has the unity of a story, and I can only answer *What am I to do?* if I can answer the prior question *Of what story or stories do I find myself a part?* We are born into roles, as a child of these parents, a citizen of this city, an heir to this tradition's debts and achievements.

Virtues, for MacIntyre, are developed in **practices**: cooperative activities like farming, chess, medicine or music, which have internal standards of excellence. Practices are housed in communities and traditions. Liberal modernity, which treats all values as private preferences, erodes them. His famous conclusion is bleak: the task is to build local forms of community within which civility and the moral life can survive the dark ages already upon us. MacIntyre, notably, rejected the label 'communitarian', since he was suspicious of the modern nation-state as a vehicle for community.

sections.heading: Rawls's Reply and Where the Debate Stands
sections.body:
Rawls did not simply repeat himself. In his 1985 essay *Justice as Fairness: Political not Metaphysical* and his book *Political Liberalism* (1993), he reframed his theory.

He now denied that justice as fairness rests on any metaphysical theory of the self. The person behind the veil is a *device of representation*, not a claim about what we really are. Its job is to model what it would be fair for free and equal citizens to agree to, given the **fact of reasonable pluralism**: under free institutions, reasonable people will inevitably come to hold different comprehensive doctrines (religious, philosophical and moral worldviews). A Catholic, a Kantian and a utilitarian can each accept liberal principles from within their own worldview, an **overlapping consensus**, without agreeing on why. In your private life you may be as encumbered as you like; in politics you appear as a free and equal citizen.

Communitarians answer that this concedes much: Rawls had narrowed liberalism's ambitions. Others argue that neutrality is impossible anyway, since every set of laws expresses some values; a 'neutral' state that permits Sunday trading or defines marriage has taken a stand.

Where does this leave us? Most participants now agree on several points. The self is socially formed; liberals no longer defend pure atomism. Communities and shared meanings matter for justice. And the communitarians were not authoritarians: Sandel, Taylor and Walzer are all democrats who value individual rights. The live question is one of balance. How much should a political community be allowed to shape its members toward a shared good, and how strongly must it protect those who wish to leave that good behind?

modernConnection.title: Post-Liberalism, Loneliness and the Return of Belonging
modernConnection.body:
The communitarian debate has escaped the academy. In *Bowling Alone* (2000) the political scientist Robert Putnam documented a long decline in American civic life: fewer people in unions, churches, parent-teacher associations and, famously, bowling leagues. He argued that this loss of **social capital** weakens democracy itself. Taylor's point that liberal freedom depends on social conditions it does not itself create reads almost like a prediction.

More recently, a group of thinkers calling themselves **post-liberal**, such as Patrick Deneen in *Why Liberalism Failed* (2018), argue that liberalism's success in freeing individuals from inherited bonds has produced loneliness, fragile families and a politics of resentment. Others, like David Goodhart in *The Road to Somewhere* (2017), describe a divide between mobile 'Anywheres', whose identities rest on achievement and portable skills, and rooted 'Somewheres', whose identities rest on place and group. That is close to Sandel's unencumbered and encumbered selves, mapped onto voting patterns.

Sandel himself, in *The Tyranny of Merit* (2020), argued that elite meritocracy tells those who do not succeed that their failure is their own fault, corroding the solidarity a democracy needs.

It is important to see where the analogy breaks down. The original communitarians were mostly social democrats who wanted richer civic life within a rights-respecting state. Some post-liberals go much further, toward a state that actively promotes a particular religious or national vision. Liberals answer that the 'communities' of the past often confined women, minorities and dissenters, and that the freedom to leave is what makes belonging a choice rather than a cage. The question you face as a citizen is the one this lesson raised: which bonds should politics nurture, and which should it merely permit?

vocabulary.term: Priority of the right over the good
vocabulary.definition: The liberal principle that fair principles of justice limit and come before any particular conception of the good life.
vocabulary.example: Because of the priority of the right over the good, the state may not ban a religion even if most citizens find it misguided.

vocabulary.definition: The view that government should not favour any one conception of the good life over others.
vocabulary.example: Funding museums raised questions about state neutrality, since not every citizen values high art.

vocabulary.definition: Sandel's label for a self conceived as prior to and independent of all its ends and attachments.
vocabulary.example: The unencumbered self chooses its loyalties as if picking items from a menu.

vocabulary.definition: A commitment or relationship that is part of who a person is, not merely something they possess or chose.
vocabulary.example: For many people, their mother tongue is a constitutive attachment rather than a preference.

vocabulary.definition: Walzer's ideal that each social good is distributed by its own principle, so no one good dominates the others.
vocabulary.example: Complex equality is violated when wealth buys political office.

vocabulary.definition: A trade that a just society forbids because it would let one good (usually money) invade another sphere.
vocabulary.example: Selling your vote is a blocked exchange in a democracy.

vocabulary.definition: Rawls's claim that free societies will always contain reasonable people with conflicting religious and moral worldviews.
vocabulary.example: Given reasonable pluralism, laws cannot be justified by appeal to one church's teaching.

vocabulary.definition: Agreement on political principles reached by people who endorse them for different reasons from within their own worldviews.
vocabulary.example: Religious and secular citizens may join an overlapping consensus on free speech.

thinkingExercise.title: Mapping Your Encumbrances
thinkingExercise.prompt: Test Sandel's and Kymlicka's claims against your own life. Which of your commitments could you revise without ceasing to be yourself, and what would that tell you about the state's proper role?
steps: List six commitments or attachments: some chosen (a hobby, a career), some inherited (a language, a family, a place, perhaps a faith).
For each, ask: could I give this up and still be recognisably me? Mark each as 'revisable' or 'constitutive'.
Pick one constitutive attachment. Was there ever a moment when you questioned it? Does the fact that you could question it support Kymlicka's reply?

Now consider one public policy that bears on such attachments (for example, state funding for minority-language schools, or a national service programme). Should a liberal state support it? Write a paragraph arguing each side.

summary: Liberals like Rawls defend the priority of the right over the good and state neutrality among conceptions of the good life.
Sandel argued that liberalism presupposes an unencumbered self and cannot account for constitutive attachments and unchosen obligations.
Taylor argued that autonomy depends on social conditions and that identity is dialogical, grounding a politics of recognition.
Walzer replaced universal principles with shared social meanings and complex equality; MacIntyre diagnosed modern moral language as fragments of lost traditions.
Rawls's Political Liberalism recast his theory as political, not metaphysical, resting on an overlapping consensus amid reasonable pluralism.

quiz.question: What does 'the priority of the right over the good' mean?
options: Rights matter more than happiness in every case
Principles of justice set limits within which people pursue their own conceptions of the good
The state should promote the best way of life
Individuals have a right to whatever they think is good
quiz.explanation: Justice sets a fair framework first; particular visions of the good life must operate within it.

quiz.question: Sandel's term 'constitutive attachments' refers to:
options: Laws written into a constitution
Contracts freely entered
Commitments that partly make up who a person is
Attachments to material goods
quiz.explanation: Constitutive attachments are not merely possessions of the self but part of its identity.

quiz.question: Kymlicka's reply to Sandel is that liberals need only claim we can question any particular commitment, not all of them at once.
quiz.explanation: Kymlicka argues that the capacity to revise any given end is real and is what liberalism protects.

quiz.question: Taylor's argument against atomism holds that:
options: Individuals are fully self-sufficient
The capacity for autonomy develops only within certain kinds of society, which we therefore have reason to sustain
Rights should always trump obligations
Atoms are the basis of political science
quiz.explanation: If autonomy depends on social conditions, valuing autonomy means valuing the community that makes it possible.

quiz.question: Which situation is the clearest violation of Walzer's complex equality?
options: A doctor treating the sickest patients first
A writer winning a prize for the best novel
A billionaire buying a seat in parliament
Two people trading books they own
quiz.explanation: Money invading the sphere of political office is exactly the domination Walzer opposes.

quiz.question: MacIntyre's parable of a world where science survives only in fragments is meant to illustrate:
options: The danger of technology
The state of modern moral language, used without the traditions that gave it meaning
Why physics is more reliable than ethics
The superiority of Enlightenment reason
quiz.explanation: He argues our moral vocabulary is a set of fragments from older frameworks, explaining why moral debates seem interminable.

quiz.question: MacIntyre enthusiastically accepted the label 'communitarian' and saw the modern nation-state as the ideal community.
quiz.explanation: MacIntyre rejected the label and was suspicious of the nation-state; he favoured smaller local communities.

quiz.question: In Political Liberalism, Rawls says the original position is best understood as:
options: A device of representation modelling fair agreement among free and equal citizens
A historical event
A metaphysical account of the true self
A description of how communities actually form
quiz.explanation: Rawls denied it was a theory of the self; it models fair conditions for agreement.

quiz.question: An 'overlapping consensus' is:
options: Unanimous agreement on a single religion
Agreement among people who share every value
Agreement on political principles reached from within different worldviews
A majority vote in parliament
quiz.explanation: People with different comprehensive doctrines can each endorse liberal principles for their own reasons.

quiz.question: Most of the original communitarians, such as Sandel, Taylor and Walzer, rejected democracy and individual rights.
quiz.explanation: They were democrats who valued rights; they disputed liberalism's account of the self and of neutrality.

goDeeper.body:
One fruitful offshoot of this debate is **liberal nationalism**. Yael Tamir's *Liberal Nationalism* (1993) and David Miller's *On Nationality* (1995) argued that liberal democracies quietly depend on national identity. Why do citizens accept redistribution to strangers, or accept losing elections? Partly because they feel they share a common nationhood. If so, liberals cannot be entirely neutral about culture and identity; they need a thin, inclusive national story. Critics respond that this risks excluding immigrants and minorities, and that **constitutional patriotism** (Jürgen Habermas's idea of loyalty to democratic principles rather than to an ethnic culture) is enough.

A second offshoot is **multiculturalism**. Kymlicka's *Multicultural Citizenship* (1995) tried to reconcile liberal autonomy with group rights: minority cultures provide the 'context of choice' that makes autonomy meaningful, so liberals should sometimes protect them, for example through language rights for national minorities. But he drew a line at **internal restrictions**, when a group limits its own members' basic freedoms, as opposed to **external protections** against the larger society. Feminist critics such as Susan Moller Okin, in her essay *Is Multiculturalism Bad for Women?* (1997), warned that group rights often empower a community's most powerful members, usually older men, at the expense of women and dissenters. This debate continues around religious schools, family law and cultural practices.

readings.title: Liberalism and the Limits of Justice
readings.author: Michael Sandel
readings.note: Dense; the introduction and conclusion give the core argument against the unencumbered self.

readings.title: After Virtue
readings.author: Alasdair MacIntyre
readings.note: Chapters 1–2 (the disquieting suggestion) and 15 (narrative unity) are the essentials.

readings.title: Spheres of Justice
readings.author: Michael Walzer
readings.note: Chapter 1 sets out complex equality and the idea of blocked exchanges.

readings.title: Political Liberalism
readings.author: John Rawls
readings.note: The introduction and Lecture IV on overlapping consensus show how Rawls answered his critics.

questions: Can a state be truly neutral between ways of life, or does every set of laws favour some values?
Is the freedom to leave a community enough to make its demands legitimate, or must communities also respect members who stay and dissent?
Does a modern democracy need a shared national identity to sustain solidarity?
